*The new DineOut user flow is broadly acceptable for EE/LV/LT:*

* Bolt is no longer involved in the payment process, so there is no financial-regulation exposure.
* The entire transaction and discount application occur on the restaurant’s side; Bolt simply displays their offers and charges an agent fee.

*Core conditions I believe we should apply in EE/LV/LT:*

* Clear and easily accessible terms next to each offer (time window, minimum spend, exclusions—i.e., what is not included—and when the voucher must be shown).
* *In-app disclaimers:*
** “The final price and discount are calculated and shown on the bill by the restaurant.”
** “Show this offer before the bill is printed.”
* *T&Cs:* clearly state that the restaurant is fully responsible for the content and application of offers (in both user and partner T&Cs).

*Key risk areas in LV and LT relate to alcohol:*

Both markets have strict rules on alcohol advertising and discounts, especially:

* *LV:* discounts, loyalty promotions, or advertised price reductions for alcohol are prohibited.
* *LT:* alcohol advertising is effectively prohibited, with very narrow exceptions.

To reduce enforcement risk, *my recommended default setup for LV/LT is:*

* Legally and technically exclude alcohol from the DineOut discount base (discount applies to food only), and reflect this in the Partner T&Cs and restaurant POS settings.
* Avoid wording such as “discount on the entire bill / on drinks” — use “discount on food.”
* No alcohol imagery or alcohol-focused messages in DineOut banners or marketing.
* In Partner T&Cs, clearly shift responsibility for complying with local alcohol laws when creating offers.



Other than that, I believe we are OK to move forward with this change, thanks! 🙏

Hi [~accountid:712020:80f31809-0e9d-4c0f-8939-db5dd3d77922] / [~accountid:712020:a71e023e-7b92-450d-9731-231bc8c609d5], I’ve reviewed and analysed Greenhouse Real Talent:

h3. Legal service terms for the Greenhouse ‘Real Talent’ Beta

I agree with [~accountid:712020:341b8095-1e4f-44ea-ad93-e6b03a07da4c]'s observations, particularly regarding liability. We cannot claim anything from GH if issues arise, and the standard risks associated with a Beta apply—features lack warranties and can be withdrawn or suspended by GH at any time, affecting continuity for Bolt until proper rollout. However, since the Beta duration is short (1-3 months), the People Team could accept the terms as they are. As [~accountid:712020:341b8095-1e4f-44ea-ad93-e6b03a07da4c] mentioned, we should revisit the legal and privacy terms before any future purchase of the feature.

h3. Privacy/AI governance perspective on Real Talent

*Talent Matching feature*

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
This is the key feature of interest for the Talent Team. I reviewed the demo and approve the use of the feature *subject to the recommendations below*.
{panel}

*Compliance context*

* Greenhouse states that using this feature is at our own risk. *We must comply with the EU AI Act when using the system* — *compliance is not guaranteed.* Therefore, we must implement a process to ensure adherence to my recommendations.
* Greenhouse requires Bolt to acknowledge that the Beta Service is not intended for *high-risk purposes* — meaning it should not be used without meaningful human involvement and should not *materially influence decision-making*.

{color:#0747a6}*Recommendations*{color}

# *Train recruiters on how the matching tool works and its limitations* —
## The calibration of the tool significantly impacts the ‘Match Scores’ shown to recruiters. They should understand how it works and its effect on results.
## Recruiters need to grasp nuances to interpret Match Scores correctly. For example, configuration for calibration fields like ‘minimum years of experience’ refers to specific roles rather than overall experience. Misunderstanding this could lead to overlooking a ‘low-ranked’ candidate.
## Recruiters can manually ‘adjust’ (_update calibration_) results and should feel empowered to ‘disagree’ — we want to avoid ‘automation bias’.
# *Ensure recruiters do not overlook lower ‘match-scoring’ candidates* — The demo shows a risk that recruiters may ignore ‘low/moderate/medium’ ranked matches (at the bottom of the list) and focus solely on ‘Great/Good' matches (at the top). Under the EU AI Act, if our recruiters rely solely on the Tool for decision-making, the system would be deemed high-risk, increasing compliance obligations for both Greenhouse and Bolt.
## It is crucial for recruiters to ‘meaningfully’ engage with the results.
## Recruiters should also be encouraged to ‘adjust’ the calibration criteria, which may yield different results (a ‘weak’ candidate could become a ‘good’ candidate).

{color:#0747a6}*Actions*{color}

Regardless of the system's risk level, we have our own *data protection obligations* towards applicants.

# Applicants must be informed that Bolt uses an AI system in the recruitment process. Greenhouse has provided a draft ‘Notice’ to configure on the system, which will be shown to candidates before they apply. *Please ensure I review this wording*.
# We need to link our Recruitment Privacy Notice in the Greenhouse message sent to candidates. *The Recruitment Privacy Notice already includes high-level disclosures about our use of AI in recruitment, but we may need to update it depending on the features we enable.*

*Identity Verification feature*

* {color:#ff5630}+*We should not enable this right now*+{color} as it involves a third party (CLEAR) and likely includes _biometric data processing_ (prohibited in some countries). Let’s discuss further next year regarding where we can enable this, reconciling it with our global ‘background checks’ and ‘identity checks’.

*Fraud Detection feature*

* {color:#ff5630}*Please inform me if Bolt plans to use this feature, as it will require updates to our Recruitment Privacy Notice*{color}.
* This feature will collect and process phone numbers, IP addresses, email domain ages, locations, and other signals to deliver a ‘risk rating’ for candidates, which is a form of ‘profiling’ that we must mention in our Privacy Notice.

We replied a couple of weeks ago, and I can confirm that we have now added the information you requested to the template we use in these cases.

*About point 2 - Monitoring Fleets Balance:*
{{This is all about “Scenario 3: Execution Officer requests seizure of credits from a company (a TVDE/ride hailing fleet) and we can identify the company in the database of fleets and there are credits to be seized”}}

We were not aware that we needed to track the fleet’s balance, and after checking with the team, I can confirm that we are currently not doing this.

Following the current process and documentation, our steps are:

* Block the payout and forward the case to Commerce.
* We send a template to Commerce for approval. After they approve it, we share the response with the execution agent, indicating the fleet’s available balance and requesting the IBAN.
* Once the IBAN is provided, Commerce handles the payment. We then update the execution agent and close the case.

Commerce has also asked us to *stop sending cases without an IBAN* and to raise an SD ticket only once we have it, as sending incomplete information adds to their backlog.

Because of this, it might make sense to update the [document|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rymTsI98_2hABzNI0RQ5MdQCN2q2QbDP3atzSytLaxE/edit?tab=t.0], or even create a new flow, clearly outlining the correct steps (if scenario 3 applies):

# Block the payout.
# Ask the execution agent for the IBAN. Follow up twice, and if there is still no reply after the second attempt, close the case.
# When we receive a reply, escalate the case to Commerce with all the relevant details.
# Monitor the fleet until all payments are completed or until the execution agent advises otherwise.

This is a brief summary, but I hope it makes sense. Let me know what you think.

Thank you very much!

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The issue has now been resolved. But we still need to adjust the customer’s balance manually.
Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account? And made another refund in the amount of the refund the customer requested to their payment method as that refund also failed?

*Internal note:* *rationale for DSAR response approach*

(/) _Droit de communication_ was cleared as a valid legal basis

* The driver attached to their DSAR the exact file that Bolt previously shared with CCAS/RATP, which the driver likely received directly from the authority. As a result, the driver already has clear visibility that their personal data was disclosed to CCAS/RATP and that an investigation or official inquiry took place.
* In this context, maintaining a position of non-confirmation would not be credible or proportionate, and could undermine Bolt’s transparency obligations under GDPR. The risk of “tipping off” the data subject no longer applies, as the authority has already communicated with the driver and shared the data onward.
* For this reason, the DSAR response acknowledges that Bolt disclosed personal data to CCAS/RATP in response to a lawful request and explains Bolt’s legal obligation to cooperate with competent public authorities.
* At the same time, the response continues to restrict information that Bolt cannot lawfully provide, including the content of the authority’s request, identities or departments of public officials, and details of the authority’s mandate or investigative procedures. These elements remain protected under Articles 15(4) and 23 GDPR and relevant national law, and are outside the scope of the driver’s right of access.

Hi [~accountid:712020:dca9f9f7-c07e-426f-8cf6-5c9369581381] , 

From TP perspective, we need to apply the business model in place in Greece. According to this model, Bolt Operations OÜ provides RH online intermediation services in this country and Bolt Greece supports this operations. This campaign will be in the benefit of Bolt Operations OÜ Greek business so it makes sense that Bolt Greece is the entity signing the agreement from Bolt side. This approach is in line with [these billing guidelines|https://drive.google.com/file/d/1VB2AQBU438hOZ_TOKvoYw-VU-mGyxSe0/view] prepared in the past by Legal, Finance and Tax.

The fact that _“there are unused funds available that we can utilize for this purpose in Cyprus”_ is not a reason to have Bolt CY signing the agreement from Bolt side. Moreover, implementing pass trough transactions between Bolt subsidiaries increases manual work and workload for Accounting Team and makes more complex IC transactions traceability. If Bolt CY has cash excess, it can always be put in the Group’s cash pool structure that will ensure that other entities with cash needs can benefit from it. In its turn, Bolt CY will get an interest in exchange. Tagging [~accountid:62567ec6a872710069210b83] for visibility in the cash part.

Hope this helps.

*Internal:*

 It is very difficult to estimate the probability of risks as, being honest, this is one of most stringent provisions I've seen in Bolt Business to date. We had only a few B2G cases (e.g. public tenders) where the requirements were similar.

* *Most probable risk (~50%)*

The most likely issue is *contractual penalties (50,000 PLN per breach, plus related costs) for audit refusals*. Bolt will realistically not be able to grant the level of audit and access rights set out in the DPA. Contractually, this gives Agora a clear basis to claim penalties. The probability is high, as large business customers frequently request audits.
The primary risk is not just the penalty amount itself, but the *resource impact*: potential disputes, litigation risk, and the need to involve Privacy, Legal, and potentially external counsel, and hindered commercial relationship. In practice, these costs could approach or exceed the penalty amount.

*Possible escalation (~25%)*
Other risks may escalate beyond audits with less probability. Escalation risk largely depends on whether Agora identifies the non-compliance and chooses to escalate - via private dispute, and potentially through court proceedings or a regulatory complaint. Bolt would be incentivised to *settle*, as defending the case under the current contractual wording would be difficult and resource-intensive.If the matter were to escalate to the Polish data protection authority, the exposure would be material. For Bolt Poland, a *fine in the low-million EUR range is realistic*, with a theoretical maximum of up to *4% of global turnover*, alongside increased regulatory scrutiny.

The key recommendation is to limit Bolt’s liability and indemnity exposure, as Bolt would be in immediate and ongoing breach of contractual obligations from the moment the DPA is signed, given that we cannot comply operationally.

Hello,

After investigation with the payment service provider, we deducted that:

* Banks could show both preauthorisation + transaction completion in the bank statement. The main balance of the customer will be charged only once with the same RRN. But in their account history, customers might see two separate transactions and get confused.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

the discussion notes 17/12 for everyone visibility:

*Problem*

* Business ad attribution is incomplete because the *business ID is not generated at first entry* to the platform (it’s created only at step 3–4), miss ~90% of visitors who drop out of the self-service funnel. This prevents reliable CAC, channel and cohort reporting for self-service businesses.

*Proposed Solution*

* *Generate a hash identifier on initial entry,* replicate the driver signup approach (hash driver ID generated at signup start) to create a persistent, entry-level identifier for business visitors.
* Implement in collaboration with the web - driver signup - team, align the work with the planned sign-up page revamp, and hand reporting/data work to the business data analyst ([@srajan.kulshrestha|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U09JQQH8Q6N]) once the hash is available.

*Notes*

* The change is expected to be *relatively small from an engineering perspective*, but the real value is in *combining* the hash + promo + referral data and building the corresponding reports.
* The hash would allow identification of the ~90% top-of-funnel dropouts (e.g., ~900k of 1M visitors in a 12-month window), enabling CAC by country, touchpoint counts, cohorting and better targeting for performance marketing.
* Collab with [@srajan.kulshrestha|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U09JQQH8Q6N] and Web team on the implementation effort and post-implementation reporting. The implementation can be learned from Orkhan (Driver case).

ETA

* *Not this year* (work unlikely to complete before year-end due to holidays). The teams plan to review and coordinate in *January* and then take the task into sprint planning / implementation early next year.

*I reissued the invoice several times → But invoice still comes out with incorrect data?*

If you reissue an invoice several times and it gets fiscalised with a VAT code at least once (ie you get an invoice with a QR) → whatever newly reissued (with a different VAT code) invoices will not get fiscalised.

Therefore invoices get stuck with incorrect (old fiscalised) data.

*What is the solution?*

We investigate with the provider if there is a workaround for it. However, it is not a high priority change as of now.

*What to do now?*

From now on please make sure that you reissue invoices to the correct Data (correct VAT code).

Best regards,

Nikolay Roll

There is limitation in Jira, according to which only the *rightmost* column in a board sets Jira items as “Completed” (which is needed to remove items from sprint after completion) and “Done”. The reason why REJECT in a different column doesn’t work is because in order to remove Rejected items from the sprint, they need to Done AND Completed. If it’s in a seprate column (not rightmost), it can only be set as “Done” and therefore not completed. 

Reference: [https://support.atlassian.com/jira/kb/done-or-resolved-work-items-are-shown-as-incomplete-when-closing-sprints/|https://support.atlassian.com/jira/kb/done-or-resolved-work-items-are-shown-as-incomplete-when-closing-sprints/|smart-link] 



Fixed it by removing “REJECT” column, and mapped REJECT status to “Done” column.

From now on please make sure that you reissue invoices to the correct Data (correct VAT code).

Hi, [~accountid:712020:dc5a9fc0-ec62-423d-a2f8-435f02007669] , after reviewing the agreement, including Annex 1 – Services, please note that the document is structured as a _service access contract_ rather than a traditional lease agreement. *Annex 1* specifically outlines the types of access packages available (e.g., Partial Access, Full Access, Team Access, Day Access) and confirms that Bolt receives access rights to coworking facilities for a team of maximum 4 persons, rather than exclusive possession of a designated premises.

As such, although subleasing or transfer (RO: _subînchiriere/cesiune_) is not prohibited under the agreement and is therefore legally permissible, Bolt may only sublease or transfer its rights within the same limits established by the contract, namely, the Team Access package for up to 4 persons, and cannot grant more extensive or more favorable rights than those it currently holds.

In case a sublease agreement is concluded, I recommend including the following clauses to ensure adequate protection for Bolt:

# *Back-to-back obligations clause* – The subtenant must comply with all obligations that Bolt has under the main agreement, including rules, access limitations, and usage conditions.
# *Liability and indemnity clause* – The subtenant should assume liability for any damage caused by its personnel and indemnify Bolt for any losses arising from its use of the space.
# *Access limitation clause* – The subtenant’s access must be limited strictly to the scope permitted under the original Team Access package (maximum 4 users, coworking access only, no exclusive use).
# *No modification of space or services clause* – The subtenant may not request or implement changes to the space, services or facilities.
# *Termination alignment clause* – The sublease should automatically terminate upon termination or expiry of the main agreement, without compensation owed by Bolt.
# *No further subleasing clause* – The subtenant may not sub-sublease or otherwise transfer its rights to other parties.

I hope this is helpful.

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The issue has now been resolved. But we still need to adjust the customer’s balance manually.
Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account? And issue another refund in the amount of the refund the customer requested to their payment method as that refund also failed?

h2. 1. Documents in scope

*Dow Jones / Factiva – Bolt package*

* *Master Agreement* – “Dow Jones Master Products Terms and Conditions (US) (September 2024)”.
* *Order Form (16‑Jun‑2025)* – between Factiva Limited (Dow Jones) and Bolt Operations OÜ, which states that the Order Form and the Master Agreement together form the “Agreement”, with the Order Form prevailing in case of conflict.
* Order Form includes *Risk & Compliance feeds* (Adverse Media structured entity profiles feed; Watchlist feed) with volumes and fees.
* Order Form also contains *Additional Terms – Privacy & Risk* and a *Technical and Organisational Security Measures Schedule* (primarily imposing security requirements on Bolt as Subscriber).

DORA requires that the *full contract (including SLAs) be in one written, durable, accessible document*. Here, the “one contract” is effectively the Master + this Order Form (and its attached schedules). That structure is acceptable in principle; the issue is _what_ the combined documents contain.

----

h2. 2. Article 30(2) – Minimum contractual elements for _all_ ICT services

DORA Article 30(2) lists mandatory elements every ICT contract must contain. Here’s how the Dow Jones/Bolt Agreement measures up.

h3. (a) Clear description of all ICT services + subcontracting conditions

* The Order Form clearly describes the *services and scope*: Adverse Media and Watchlist feeds, volumes (names per annum), and complimentary access to Financial Crime Search.
* It also defines different *Risk & Compliance services / feeds* more broadly (types of feeds, structured profiles, lists, etc.).

*Subcontracting:*

* The contract gives Bolt the right to engage *Third Party Contractors* and a *Third Party Integrator (Salv)*, subject to Dow Jones approval, and makes Bolt responsible for them.
* There is *no clause that transparently addresses Dow Jones’ own sub‑outsourcing* (e.g. cloud hosting, other ICT providers), nor any approval/notification process for such subcontracting.

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(a) expects the contract to _state whether subcontracting of ICT services supporting critical or important functions is permitted and under what conditions_. This is *only partially covered*, and only for Bolt’s side (Third Party Integrators/Contractors), not Dow Jones’ own ICT sub‑providers.

----

h3. (b) Locations where services are provided and data are processed + obligation to notify changes

* The Order Form defines Bolt and Dow Jones’ *legal domiciles* (Estonia and the UK), but that is *not* the same as specifying where the ICT services are run or where data are processed.
* The Additional Terms define *“Third Country”* (essentially any country outside EEA/UK/Switzerland) for data transfer purposes and refer to EU SCC Annexes for restricted transfers.
* There is *no explicit list of regions/countries where Dow Jones hosts or processes data*, nor any *explicit obligation to notify in advance* of changes to such locations.

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(b) requires the contract to specify *regions or countries* of service delivery and data storage/processing and to require *advance notification of changes*. This is *a clear gap*.

----

h3. (c) Provisions on availability, authenticity, integrity, confidentiality of data

* The Additional Terms make Dow Jones responsible for *“adequate technical and organizational security measures”* for processing as part of the Substantive Database and servicing of Subscriber Name Requests, while Bolt is responsible for security in its own environment.
* The *Technical and Organisational Security Measures Schedule* then sets concrete controls (encryption in transit and at rest, access controls, logging, pen-testing, BC/DR, etc.) – but these measures are framed as *measures Bolt must implement* to protect Dow Jones Risk & Compliance Data.
* Dow Jones’ own service is explicitly provided “*as is*, as available” with no warranties, including no warranties that the services will operate without interruption.

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(c) requires *contractual provisions on availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality* of data. You have good coverage on *confidentiality* and some on *integrity*, but essentially *no contractual commitments on availability*, and what exists is heavily disclaimed. This is *partially met at best*, and not in a DORA‑robust way.

----

h3. (d) Access, recovery and return of data (incl. insolvency / termination)

* Master Agreement: on termination, Bolt’s rights to use the services cease and Bolt must *purge all Information* (Dow Jones data) stored on its servers “as soon as practicable”.
* Order Form Risk & Compliance Terms: Dow Jones must _delete_ Service Results upon Bolt’s written request or upon termination, and Bolt must also purge Risk & Compliance data and Service Results from its own environment (subject to regulatory retention).

There is almost *no contractual right for Bolt to demand export/return of data from Dow Jones*, nor anything about *recovery* or *backup access* in insolvency / discontinuation scenarios.

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(d) requires provisions that *ensure access, recovery and return in an easily accessible format* of personal and non‑personal data in insolvency/termination scenarios. The Dow Jones terms focus on _deletion_ and IP restrictions, not on enabling your recovery/portability. This is *a major gap* from a DORA perspective.

----

h3. (e) Service level descriptions (including updates/revisions)

* The Order Form specifies:
** Volumes (names per year), query limits and *update frequency for the Risk & Compliance feeds* (full database daily; incremental updates daily/weekly).
* However:
** There is *no uptime/availability SLA*, no response‑time or support SLAs.
** Master Agreement explicitly *disclaims* any warranty that services will operate without interruption.

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(e) requires *service level descriptions*; for critical/important functions Article 30(3)(a) goes further and demands precise quantitative and qualitative performance targets. You have a *very limited de facto SLA (update frequency)*, but *no resilience/availability/service continuity metrics*. This is *insufficient* for DORA Article 30.

----

h3. (f) Assistance in ICT‑related incidents (costed ex‑ante)

* “Data Security Breach” is defined, and there’s a clause that *Dow Jones will notify Bolt of any Data Security Breach relating to Subscriber Name Requests and take remedial steps as required by law*.
* There is _no_ general obligation to assist Bolt with:
** Investigation of ICT incidents more broadly (e.g. availability incidents).
** Regulatory incident reporting or forensic analysis.
** And *no cost model* (e.g. “no additional cost” or pre‑agreed rates).

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(f) demands an explicit *obligation to provide assistance in ICT incidents* related to the services, *at no additional cost or a cost agreed ex ante*. The current wording is *narrow (only personal‑data breaches) and not costed*. Only *partially aligned*.

----

h3. (g) Cooperation with competent and resolution authorities

* Additional Terms: *In case of inspection or audit by a public authority*, each party must provide “all reasonable assistance” to the other in responding, subject to necessary regulatory consents.

This is positive but:

* It’s framed as *mutual assistance between Bolt and Dow Jones*, not as a direct, unconditional obligation by Dow Jones to “fully cooperate with Bolt’s competent and resolution authorities”.

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(g) requires an obligation on the ICT provider to *fully cooperate with competent and resolution authorities*. The mutual‑assistance language is *helpful but too generic and conditional*, and not clearly framed from the DORA perspective.

----

h3. (h) Termination rights and minimum notice periods

* Master Agreement: termination for breach (30‑day cure, then immediate) and for insolvency events.
* Order Form: subscription term is 12 months with *3‑month prior written notice* for cancellation at end of initial or renewal term.

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(h) and Recital 71 require *termination rights and appropriate notice periods*. On pure contract mechanics, this is broadly *acceptable*, but Article 28(7) (below) adds more specific ICT‑risk triggers that are not reflected.

----

h3. (i) Conditions for participation in your ICT security awareness / DORA training

* The Agreement is *silent* on Dow Jones’ participation in Bolt’s ICT security awareness or digital operational resilience training.

🔎 *DORA position:* Article 30(2)(i), read together with Article 13(6), expects *conditions for the ICT provider’s participation in your ICT security & resilience training*. This is *missing*.

----

h2. 3. Article 30(3) – Extra requirements where services support _critical or important functions_

Given these feeds support AML/KYC screening, there is a strong argument they underpin a *“critical or important function”* under DORA. If treated as such, Article 30(3) adds more requirements:

h3. (a) Full SL descriptions with quantitative & qualitative performance targets

* As noted, no uptime/downtime, RTO/RPO, incident response times, or support SLAs are defined – only feed update frequency and volumes.

➡️ *Not met.* You’d need explicit SLAs for availability, latency, support response, recovery objectives, etc.

----

h3. (b) Notice and reporting obligations on developments affecting service delivery

* For content/services Dow Jones does not own, the Master says that if service provision must cease, Dow Jones will give reasonable prior notice and either provide substitutes or terminate and refund pre‑paid fees.
* There is *no broader obligation* to notify:
** material developments impacting Dow Jones’ ability to provide services (e.g. major incidents, regulatory issues, critical vulnerabilities);
** significant changes in controls or risk profile.

➡️ *Only partially met* (limited to service discontinuation, not a general DORA‑style notification duty).

----

h3. (c) Requirement to implement and test business continuity and ICT security measures

* Data/privacy terms: Dow Jones is responsible for implementing *adequate technical and organisational security measures* but with limited detail.
* The detailed *Technical & Organisational Measures Schedule* is largely aimed at Bolt’s environment, not Dow Jones’ own ICT estate.
* No *explicit promises* by Dow Jones to maintain/test its own ICT business continuity plans, nor to comply with specific standards (ISO 27001, SOC 2, etc.).

➡️ *Partially met* for security, *missing* for business continuity/testing.

----

h3. (d) Participation and cooperation in TLPT (threat‑led penetration testing)

* The Agreement is *silent* on Dow Jones’ cooperation in your TLPT under DORA Articles 26–27.
* The only “pen testing” obligation is on Bolt: you must conduct penetration tests of your own environment and share high‑level results with Dow Jones on request.

➡️ *Not met*. There is no contractual obligation for Dow Jones to support TLPT on the integrated service.

----

h3. (e) Rights to monitor and audit (financial entity & authorities)

DORA wants broad ongoing monitoring rights, including:

* unrestricted rights of access, inspection and audit by the financial entity and competent authorities;
* obligation for the provider to fully cooperate in those onsite inspections and audits.

In the Agreement:

* *Audit rights flow the other way*: Dow Jones can require Bolt to provide records and server data to verify licence compliance.
* Only audit‑like obligation on Dow Jones is the narrow “reasonable assistance in responding to audits by a public authority” clause.

➡️ *Major gap*: there are *no explicit audit/inspection/data‑center access rights for Bolt or its competent authorities*, nor alternative assurance mechanisms.

----

h3. (f) Exit strategies, transition period, migration assistance

DORA requires exit provisions including a *mandatory adequate transition period* during which the provider continues services at agreed SLA levels to allow smooth migration.

Here:

* Termination/expiry simply stops service and forces Bolt to purge Dow Jones data.
* No obligation on Dow Jones to:
** continue services for a defined transition period;
** assist in migration to alternative providers or in‑house systems;
** support data portability beyond very limited contexts.

➡️ *Not met*. The Agreement does not support the kind of exit strategy DORA expects.

----

h2. 4. Article 28 – General principles and specific contract‑related points

Most of Article 28 is *internal* to the financial entity (strategy, risk register, due diligence, etc.). But some points are clearly *implemented via contract*:

h3. 28(5) – Only contract with providers that comply with appropriate information security standards

* There is *no express representation* by Dow Jones that it complies with “appropriate information security standards” or with “most up‑to‑date and highest quality” standards for critical/important functions.
* You do have:
** General “adequate technical and organizational measures” wording for Dow Jones.
** Detailed security measures that _you_, as Bolt, must implement.

➡️ From a DORA audit perspective, this makes it hard to *demonstrate Dow Jones meets 28(5)*. A specific commitment (e.g. to ISO 27001, SOC 2, or equivalent) would be helpful.

----

h3. 28(7) – Termination triggers linked to ICT‑risk findings

Financial entities must ensure contractual arrangements can be terminated where, among other things:

* the provider seriously breaches law/contract terms;
* monitoring reveals circumstances that may alter performance of the outsourced functions;
* weaknesses in provider’s ICT risk management are evidenced;
* supervision by the competent authority is hindered.

In the Agreement:

* Termination for *breach* and *insolvency* is covered.
* However, there are *no explicit termination rights*:
** for documented weaknesses in Dow Jones’ ICT risk management or inability to ensure data availability/integrity/confidentiality;
** where competent authorities say their supervision is hindered by the arrangement.

➡️ *Partially aligned* (generic breach/insolvency), but *missing DORA‑specific triggers.*

----

h3. 28(8) – Exit strategies for ICT services supporting critical or important functions

DORA requires *documented exit strategies and transition plans* and the ability to exit without disrupting business, breaching regulations, or degrading client service.

* As noted under Article 30(3)(f), the Agreement lacks:
** contractual exit assistance,
** transitional service obligations,
** data portability/transfer commitments.

➡️ While DORA puts the obligation on *Bolt* to have exit strategies, the *contract doesn’t give you the tools* to do so smoothly, which is problematic if the services are classified as critical/important.

----

h2. 5. Overall assessment & practical next steps

h3. Overall

* The current Dow Jones Master + Order Form *does not fully satisfy* DORA Articles 30 and 28 as a contract for ICT services supporting critical or important functions.
* It does cover:
** description of the services and volumes;
** some data‑protection responsibilities and data‑breach notification;
** basic termination and notice periods.
* But it *falls short* on several key DORA contractual elements, notably:
** Clear statement of *data locations* and *change‑notification*;
** *Provider‑side subcontracting* transparency and conditions;
** *SLAs* on availability and performance;
** Robust *data access/recovery/return & portability* rights;
** Broad *incident‑assistance* obligations (with pre‑agreed costs);
** Strong *regulatory cooperation* wording;
** *Audit/inspection rights* for Bolt and its competent/resolution authorities;
** *TLPT cooperation*;
** *Exit/transition assistance* and mandatory transition period;
** *Training participation* commitments;
** DORA‑specific *termination triggers* linked to ICT‑risk findings.

h3. Suggested remediation (at a high level)

In practice, these gaps are usually addressed via:

# *DORA addendum / side letter with Dow Jones*
A separate schedule that:
#* Mirrors Article 30(2)–(3) wording (especially for data locations, SLAs, audit rights, exit strategies, TLPT, training, incident assistance, cooperation with authorities).
#* Introduces DORA‑aligned *termination triggers* per Article 28(7).
#* Clarifies *information security standards* used by Dow Jones (ISO, SOC, etc.) to evidence 28(5).
# *Internal DORA documentation*
Even with contract gaps, you’ll need to ensure your internal ICT third‑party risk framework and register of ICT arrangements under Article 28 are up to date for this provider, including classification (is this a critical/important function?) and concentration‑risk analysis.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

For cases where refund was issued but can’t be seen on the user’s card or Bolt balance.

* Check where the refund was sent to and if it was successful on the [transaction history page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/user-balance/trxHistory?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A%2225%22%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22target_account_id%22%3A%2265766018%22%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn] with the correct user ID 
** If Bolt balance refund is successful, there is a green button after the refund “🟢 success”
** If refund to card, 💳 success
* Check if the payment method used to make the order is not a business account. In this case, the refund will be sent to the business account balance.
* Check if the user did not spend their refund on a next order (or orders) for Bolt balance refunds
* Check if the user did not have a previous debt or previous failed payment that was covered up with the refund
* If refund was sent to Balance instead of card, check first if payment was made from card. Usually, if card payment fails, card refund also fails. Sometimes refund will be sent to balance in cases payment was charged from balance first as debt and the refund will clear the debt previously created by the balance charge. 
* Check [payment page|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/1946767063], to ensure there are no errors on the refund and advise the user to check with their bank if card refund was successfully completed.
** If there is an error, escalate to Commerce > Ride Hailing/Food/Rentals payments
* Only successful card payments can be refunded to card.

Hello,

The customer used an APM (Alternative Payment Method) to place the order and this type of payment methods does not have a preauthorisation option that is later reversed. They only support a direct charge on the card. So if the user makes an order but then cancels it, in this case we refund their money unlike preauthorisation where we just release the reserved amount. 
So in this case, the user placed an order and we charged them higher, but at the end of the ride, the order price decreased or the order is cancelled, so automatically we refunded them the difference. But later on from your end (CS) you initiated a full refund, which was applied to the first higher order amount. And this is what creates the debt as the balance thinks that we have returned the full amount to the user, meaning whatever the user previously paid was all returned to them. But since a service was provided to the user for the order or cancellation fee, it is still trying to charge the user for the extra refunded amount. That is where the debt comes from.

The issue has now been resolved. But we still need to adjust the customer’s balance manually.
Could you complete a refund to the user’s balance on a different order to compensate for the debt in their account? And issue another refund in the amount of the refund the customer requested to their payment method as that refund also failed?

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Afiba

* the purpose, controller details, data retention period, and a reference to a privacy notice are made available; and

However, you remain accountable for ensuring compliance with data protection law and for any breaches arising from your or your drivers’ actions.
Please confirm once you have reviewed the situation and taken the necessary steps in response to this report.
If you have any questions or require further clarification, please don’t hesitate to contact us.
Kind regards,

I've checked and it is because the is the arbitrary limit of 25 last cases being fetched, with the “last cases” being all cases sorted by last_update (open and closed). So if there were 25+ cases that were closed afterwards any open case was updated, no open cases would show up. 

We could theoretically fix it by fetching open and closed cases separately (esp. that the customer-support API already offers filtering by status), but in practice it wouldn't be so easy, as the list is already fetched by webview upon opening the landing page (to display the recent cases), and it would mess up the (already fragile) logic of shouldRefreshList which relies on unread cases and other signals. 

Considering that there is no easy and quick fix to mitigate, I would vote for closing this in favor of [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/SUPX-1264|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/SUPX-1264|smart-link]

# There is no practical alternative to using an edge protection service, as we require volumetric DDoS protection before traffic reaches our infrastructure and applications.
# Since the decision to stay with or move away from Cloudflare is not owned by InfoSec, the focus should be on maximizing the value of the existing Enterprise subscription:
## If switching providers is not currently an option, enabling annual billing should be considered, as it can reduce costs by ~20%.
## To improve protection against SMS pumping and advanced bot abuse, Cloudflare needs to expose more actionable signals to the application layer to support better decision-making.
## Developers should be enabled to add or customize edge rules (with appropriate guardrails), without requiring direct involvement from security teams for every change.
# If there is interest in evaluating alternatives, AWS WAF would be the preferred candidate:
The current infrastructure already runs on AWS, reducing integration and operational risk.
## Moving to AWS WAF would eliminate reliance on an external edge provider and reduce exposure to unexpected Cloudflare outages or performance degradations.
## Any migration would require careful planning due to architectural specifics, such as the current use of Network Load Balancers (NLBs), that do not support AWS WAF.
## AWS offers a reasonably priced security stack (WAF + Shield Advanced) that can provide WAF capabilities comparable to what we use today, while reducing third-party dependency risk.

the discussion notes 17/12 for everyone visibility:

*Problem*

* Business ad attribution is incomplete because the *business ID is not generated at first entry* to the platform (it’s created only at step 3–4), miss ~90% of visitors who drop out of the self-service funnel. This prevents reliable CAC, channel and cohort reporting for self-service businesses.

*Proposed Solution*

* *Generate a hash identifier on initial entry,* replicate the driver signup approach (hash driver ID generated at signup start) to create a persistent, entry-level identifier for business visitors.
* Implement in collaboration with the web - driver signup - team, align the work with the planned sign-up page revamp, and hand reporting/data work to the business data analyst ([@srajan.kulshrestha|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U09JQQH8Q6N]) once the hash is available.

*Notes*

* The change is expected to be *relatively small from an engineering perspective*, but the real value is in *combining* the hash + promo + referral data and building the corresponding reports.
* The hash would allow identification of the ~90% top-of-funnel dropouts (e.g., ~900k of 1M visitors in a 12-month window), enabling CAC by country, touchpoint counts, cohorting and better targeting for performance marketing.
* Collab with [@srajan.kulshrestha|https://bolt.enterprise.slack.com/team/U09JQQH8Q6N] and Web team on the implementation effort and post-implementation reporting. The implementation can be learned from Orkhan (Driver case).

_Hence our insistence on not adding any element that might suggest that we are responding to requirements arising from Articles 26 or 28 of the GDPR. Especially since the CNIL is not bound by the terms of the contract._

_This is why we have proposed instead to include in the contract a clause referring to the principle of good cooperation between the parties.”_

Our legal department therefore proposes to maintain the principle of good cooperation between the parties, to ensure the principle of data exchange between distinct data controllers is respected.

here is summary of Privacy review of the DPA 

* *Indemnity & Liability*

Liability is fully subject to the Terms’ caps; no carve‑outs for data protection breaches. 6 months fees does not provide reasonable cover for breach of confidentiality, data protection obligations, and security incidents/regulatory fines.

* *Training models*

DPA does not contain *explicit prohibition* on training models on Client Data. Annex 2 mentions “Controls for Implementing AI/ML,” but this is programmatic, not a contractual use restriction. Absent a ban, “provide and maintain the Services” could be interpreted to include product improvement/feature development. We need to ask for a contractual prohibition on using Client Data for model training or third‑party AI unless explicitly opted‑in.

* *Unilateral Changes to the DPA*

Pipedrive may *unilaterally modify* the DPA “_to comply_” or to “_reflect changes in its data processing practices_,” effective upon *posting*; continued use = acceptance. We should sign a separate DPA and do not rely on online terms.

* *Personal Data Breach*

Notice timeline: “Without undue delay (*targeted* notification time of no greater than 72 business hours)”. Risk: “_Targeted_” is non‑binding and “Business hours” can stretch beyond GDPR expectations (72 hours). Hard cap of 48 hours (not business hours) is preferred.

Can we create criteria for branding viability? *From a reclassification perspective, it is important to distinguish clearly between preferences that relate to the vehicle and preferences that relate to the driver’s way of working. Focusing on higher-quality cars is generally acceptable. Vehicle-based criteria are typically understood as service-quality requirements rather than as control over drivers. Selecting cars based on objective features such as model, condition, emissions class, or comfort level does not, in itself, affect driver autonomy and is therefore unlikely to raise employment classification concerns.*
*The concept of preferring “full-time drivers,” however, requires more caution. The reclassification risk tends to increase where drivers are implicitly or explicitly encouraged to work continuously, regularly, or predominantly on one platform. Even without formal obligations, favouring drivers who work full time can be interpreted as creating expectations around availability, continuity, or economic dependence. If such a preference results in drivers feeling incentivised to structure their working time around the platform, it may contribute to a perception that the platform is organising how the work is performed rather than simply offering opportunities.*
** Also ideally we do Branding with Tiering, according to achieved KPIs, is this possible? *Branding tiering based on KPIs can be more sensitive from a reclassification standpoint, depending on how the KPIs are designed and used. The main risk arises when KPIs are tied to driver behaviour or performance in a way that resembles performance management. Metrics such as acceptance rates, cancellation behaviour, ride volumes, availability levels, or similar indicators can be perceived as tools to steer or discipline how drivers work, especially if meaningful benefits are attached to them.*
*If branding tiering becomes a mechanism that rewards drivers for behaving in certain ways or meeting productivity-style targets, it may be seen as reducing driver autonomy and increasing the platform’s influence over day-to-day work. This is particularly relevant where branding carries economic value, visibility advantages, or cost savings for drivers, as it strengthens the link between performance and dependency on the platform.*
*That said, tiering is less problematic where it is clearly disconnected from behavioural control. For example, tiering linked to objective, non-behavioural factors—such as vehicle specifications, safety features, or compliance standards—poses a lower risk. The closer tiering comes to influencing how drivers organise their time, accept work, or prioritise the platform, the higher the reclassification exposure.*

If possible, there is another *inefficiency* to address here 😅 

You see, in [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/DPM-2277|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/DPM-2277|smart-link], we implemented logic in {{delivery-store-translations}} that acts as follows:

#  When translation set/bulkSet endpoint is invoked, check if there are any _actual_ mutations.
# If there are mutations, run the “amend AI metadata” logic for these mutations.

Now, here is what happens during every PIM sync:

# PIM sync logic tries to update a particular entity
# This triggers the mutation check logic in {{delivery-store-translations}} (through a chain of internal calls)
# Metadata is updated by the mutation check → apply metadata updates logic
# Metadata is _then_ updated again to the correct value by the sync logic

So between 2-4, we have a very brief window where the data is inconsistent (the automated {{set}}/{{setBulk}} is treated as a “human-driven” change).

Then 4 corrects the situation.

_How could this be solved?_
Well, I think the only way to do it is to add an additional input for the translations {{set}}/{{setBulk}} APIs. One that indicates whether the action is human-initiated or not.

The annoying part is that this would need to be dragged through several layers → PIM UI → WMS controller → PIM service → Translations service.

But I am not convinced there is a better way to do it, for now.

Privacy team reviewed the PDPA data protection clause (Section 6). Overall, the structure and intent are broadly acceptable and generally align with our updated BB T&Cs. The clause does not expressly appoint Bolt as a processor and recognises controller responsibilities under applicable law.

That said, a small number of provisions required alignment with Bolt’s standard data-sharing practices, including:

* clarification that both parties act as independent data controllers,
* replacing consent-only processing language with a lawful-basis approach under applicable law,
* adjusting breach notification timing from “immediate” to “without undue delay”,
* aligning retention and deletion obligations with each party’s independent legal and operational requirements, and
* confirming that liability remains governed by the underlying agreement rather than creating a standalone data-protection liability regime.

I have implemented those updated in the [English draft|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O5QjoAjIi1fMdCjQpvSc2WhYau7qU3pMDUbaCP08UYo/edit?usp=sharing]. Subject to these limited, targeted updates, the clause is acceptable and consistent with Bolt’s data-sharing and compliance framework.

** ENG seems to think that Alina and Alla could be “_the same person or they are close friends or family members_”, but I have not seen much to support this theory.
* Account details change history:
** The account at issue ([Account 1|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/55973114/overview]) was originally set up in 2020 under phone number +37127533341 (“*Phone 1*”).
*** It is unclear whose details were originally on Account 1.
** In January 2022, there was a login via Phone 1, but via a new Apple Device {{D13E7D77-AC0E-49DE-A19A-612DEA8A2388}} (“*Apple Device*”). 
** From November 2023, there were logins via the same Apple Device, but a different phone number: +37125199833 (“*Phone 2*”).
*** This login was by Alina Guseva. We can assume this because: (i) [Account 2|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/255027998/overview], set up under the Apple Device and Phone 2, is under Alina’s name; and (ii) in May 2024 (when the Apple Device still had access), the details on Account 1 were changed to those of Alina’s.
** In November 2024, there was another login via Phone 2, but this time via Android Device {{ffu5p0EIS0ijaGmN3Od6Au}} (“*Android* *Device*”).
*** This login was by Alla Grinberg. We can assume this because: (i) [Account 3|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/255056798/overview], set up under the Android Device, is under Alla’s name; and (ii) in December 2025 (when the Apple Device was permanently logged out), the details on Account 1 were changed to those of Alla’s.
*** If any phone number recycling occurred, this is probably the place when it did.
** On 7 March 2025, there was another login via the Android Device, but a different phone number: +46793513614 (“*Phone 3*”).
*** i.e., Unknown/Phone 1  → Phone 1/Apple → Apple/Phone 2 → Phone 2/Android → Android/Phone 3.
*** Between December 2024 and March 2025, both devices had access to Account 1 (during this time, the only orders came from the Android Device). 
*** The Apple Device was permanently logged out on 7 March (around the same time as Account 2 as created). This was the same day that the Android Device created Account 3.
*** Currently, only the Android Device and Phone 3 are active on Account 1 (Alla).
* CONCLUSION:
** It seems likely that this is a case of phone number recycling (in Nov 2024), but ENG also thinks it is possible that these users could be the same person / that they know one another. Until this is confirmed, we cannot yet be confident of unauthorised access / a data breach.
* NEXT STEPS:
** Ask ENG to try and clarify: (i) Who originally created Account 1; (ii) Can we track at what point(s) Alina and Alla had access to Account 1; (iii) Is there anything further we can do on our side to confirm if these are the same person; and (iv) If we archived Account 1, would it be correct to say that Alina could continue using Bolt via Account 2 and Alla could continue using Bolt via Account 3? ([Link|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C06R63EQ6CS/p1766413919562139?thread_ts=1766067628.271829&cid=C06R63EQ6CS])
** Get CS to message Alla and confirm if they recognise the name ‘Alina G’ (do not give full name). If they do not, this lends weight to us dealing with two separate users here.
** If we can be confident of unauthorised access / phone number recycling, then we can: (a) archive Account 1; and (b) offer the affected users a copy of their data.

Hi [~accountid:5d8df399c7d4e30dc2836580] In the UK, VAT registration is a driver obligation based on individual taxable turnover. Bolt cannot be seen to direct, require, or steer drivers towards VAT registration, as this would materially increase employment misclassification risk and VAT principal risk (i.e. arguments that Bolt is the supplier rather than an agent).

That said, there is scope to support drivers in a neutral and optional way, provided clear boundaries are respected.

* Provide neutral, factual information about VAT (e.g. thresholds, voluntary vs mandatory registration), ideally by linking to HMRC guidance, with clear disclaimers that this is not tax advice.
* Run general educational campaigns or webinars (open to all drivers) framed as “understanding VAT for self-employed drivers”, without nudging, deadlines, or earnings-based targeting.
* Offer optional discounts for third-party accounting/tax tools, provided:
** participation is opt-in,
** there is no Bolt integration,
** drivers have genuine choice,
** Bolt does not receive or rely on outputs.

What Bolt should not do (high risk):

* Push or prompt VAT registration based on driver earnings data.
* Present VAT registration as expected or required to continue using the platform.
* Integrate VAT registration or VAT return processes into Bolt systems.
* Act as an intermediary managing or monitoring drivers’ VAT compliance.

+*UPDATE (22.12)*+

*General:*

* WfW has launched in Nuremberg, as a pilot. Intention is to roll it out further across Germany.
** To implement this, we are partnering with a local fleet. WfW will be launched as a new category (G-Cars for Women).
** In Germany, passports have gender field on them (but not drivers licences / ID cards).
* Generally, this is ok from a privacy POV. The main concern is with verification (i.e., proportionality of verification, and what we do with gender-fluid data subjects).

*Rider Verification:*

* Process:
** *Document*: We will be collecting a copy of the rider’s passport (the only doc to have a gender field on it), and then comparing the picture against a selfie.
** *Automation/Consent*: In cases of exact matches, this system is fully automated; otherwise, there are fallbacks of human review for inconclusive results.
*** Sudipto has provided [this|https://www.figma.com/design/GJfajTTxosdcPKRaLZbv7k/Dash-s-Sandbox-2024?node-id=0-1&p=f&t=ulJr741bWjFOk93X-0] user flow. However, this refers to keeping account secure, so I am not sure it is correct.
** *Checks*: We are looking at both a face match and the gender field - the latter is a more recent development (see [+here+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/PRODWIKI/pages/5737709569/Sex-field+Check+for+Woman-Only+Category+v2]).
*** Unverified riders = ID verification + selfie (face match) + sex field check.
**** Veritas will perform the following checks: (i) Is the document real? (ii) Is it a real face? (iii) Does the selfie match the passport photo? (iv) Does the ID document have a field containing sex? (v) Is the gender listed as female? If these are all passed, then the rider can use WfW.
*** Verified riders = If sex field is female, then no changes (i.e., rider can continue to use WfW without interruption). if sex field is blank, rider is prompted to verify their sex in order to continue. If sex is not listed as female, then rider cannot continue to use WfW.
** *Third parties*: We are not relying on third-party verification processes. Manual checks are done by outsourced agents, but the technology is in-house.
** *Retention*: We are keeping the copies in AWS S3 buckets (in the EU). The retention period is currently set at 1 year.
*** Once the records are deleted, the only thing that remains is the ‘legal_sex’ listed in the account details history (see e.g., [+this view+|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/201834537/history?tz=Europe%2FTallinn&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D]).
* Thoughts:
** ⚠️ Legal basis: 
*** From a quick skim, it looks like *consent* may be needed. There are specific laws on copying ID docs (e.g., [+ID Law+|https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_pauswg/englisch_pauswg.html#p0185]), and biometric processing will be involved here. As such, we would need to ask for consent. I still need to *check the user flow* to see if consent / manual options are genuinely offered.
*** If consent not given, then we would need to: (i) do manual checks instead of biometric (which are in place already); and (ii) potentially not allow the rider to use WfW at all if passports are the only way of verifying (which sounds like this is the case). Ultimately, *this should probably be checked with local counsel*.
** ⚠️ Proportionality: 
*** Although this is a grey area, we can argue that checking the ID doc is proportionate, as otherwise there is not ‘official’ way to verify gender - we would effectively just be eyeballing it (other methods would not yield the same results). 
*** However, we may need to be careful with how we *_retain_* this data (ideal approach would be to extract the gender field and delete the rest. If we keep it, it must be clearly marked as a copy). 1 year may be a proportionate period, however *this will depend on what local counsel says*.
** ⚠️ Transparency: 
*** We need to ensure we are being specific and clear on why we are asking the rider for their passport, and what we will do with it. *This will depend on the user flow*.
** ⚠️ ADM: 
*** We can argue this does not meet the threshold, as riders can use other categories (and human review element). However, the system should be robustly designed to avoid errors.
** ⚠️ Discrimination: 
*** Gender is fluid, so some people may not identify with the gender listed in their passport. There is no easy solution to this - although not strictly a privacy issue, if we take a purposive approach to the feature, then we cannot allow them to use the category. They can use other categories instead.

*Driver Verification:*

* Process:
** *Document / Checks / Automation*: It seems that we will be verifying drivers based on a mixture of: (i) what they specify during the registration flow (see [+LSS-58536+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-58536]), which is specific to WfW; and, more relevantly (ii) reviewing ID docs provided by the drivers.
** *Third parties*: It seems that we are reviewing these (we are not relying on the fleet to do so).
* Thoughts:
** Same as above. Riders are higher risk here on proportionality grounds; otherwise legal analysis is pretty much the same.

+*LOCAL LAW ANALYSIS - PROCESSING PASSPORTS*+

* *Collection*: It does not appear that German laws prevent us from asking for a photo of a driver’s / rider’s passport in this context (as the purpose here is technically identification). However, local ID/passport laws require us to rely on the user’s *consent* for the “copy” of the passport, and to process data relating to it. This is _in addition to_ biometric processing consent.
** Under [s20(2) PAuswG|https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/pauswg/__20.html]: “_The ID card may only be photocopied by the cardholder or by other persons with the consent of the cardholder in such a way that the photocopy is clearly and permanently recognizable as a copy…_ I_f personal data from the identity card is collected or processed by means of photocopying, the data collection or processing agency may only do so with the consent of the cardholder_”.
*** NB. Reproductions in this context are considered as both photocopies and photographs ([link|https://www.personalausweisportal.de/Webs/PA/EN/citizens/german-id-card/copies_of_your_identity_documents/copies_of_your_identity_documents-node.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com]).
*** Otherwise, general principles from the DPR apply re data minimisation etc.
** Under [s18(3) PassG |https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/pa_g_1986/__18.html](Passport Act): “_The passport may only be copied by the passport holder or by other persons with the passport holder's consent, provided that the copy is clearly and permanently identifiable as such. Persons other than the passport holder may not disclose the copy to third parties unless disclosure is for the purpose of applying for a visa for the passport holder and the passport holder has consented to the disclosure. If personal data from the passport is collected or processed by means of copying, the data-collecting or data-processing entity may only do so with the passport holder's consent. The provisions of general data protection law concerning the collection and use of personal data remain unaffected_.”
** NB. The above appears to be separate to asking for consent to biometric processing - We still need to do this under A9 GDPR. As such, we should likely take the following approach:
*** (i) Say as part of the user flow that by providing a photo of the passport, the user consents to us processing it. Flag that this consent can be withdrawn at any time. If the user does not provide their consent, or subsequently withdraws it, then they can no longer use the category.
*** (ii) _Separately_, ask for the user’s consent to biometric processing of the ID/selfie. If user does not provide this, then we revert to manual verification.
** NB. Under s20(3) PAuswG: “_The serial numbers may not be used with the aid of automated procedures to retrieve or link personal data_”. As such, we need to be extra careful to not extract this.
*** Same goes for s18(12) PassG: “_Serial numbers must not be used in such a way as to enable the retrieval of personal data from files or the linking of files._”
* *Retention*: It seems likely that the most compliant approach would be to only retain the name, photo and gender field in the photo of the ID (everything else should be redacted ASAP). Alternatively, if we retain it, then per PAuswG we must clearly mark the image as a copy.
** German public guidance states that it is often enough to note “presented/verified” rather than retaining a full copy of the ID . Once a copy has fulfilled its purposes, it should be deleted / redacted ([link|https://www.personalausweisportal.de/Webs/PA/EN/citizens/german-id-card/copies_of_your_identity_documents/copies_of_your_identity_documents-node.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com]).
** NB. We probably have stronger grounds to retain full driver IDs than we do rider IDs.
* NB. We cannot share the photo of the passport with third parties without the user’s consent.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions for Sudipto:
** Driver verification:
*** So we are effectively re-using ID docs already gained during registration, and the FO is not contributing to verification?
*** Is the ID doc verification / review process for drivers the same as for riders? In particular re things to check, automations, in-house tools etc?
** Rider verification:
*** Are you sure this is for riders / WfW? The linked user flow talks about keeping the user’s account safe, so does not seem directly applicable here. I need to see the: (i) the explanation we give re why we are collecting these datapoints and what we are checking; and (ii) the consent wording/option/alternatives.
* Questions for local counsel:
** 1. Is consent needed to collect and store passports (even if the passport holder is technically the one taking the photo/making the copy before sending it to Bolt? Can we assume consent at the point the user provides the photo?)? Is this separate to biometric processing consent?
** 2. Is passport collection/_storage_ _of one year_ likely to be disproportionate in this context (for IDs and selfies)? Do we need to redact everything beyond name, face and gender?
** 3. Are there any fields on the passport that could raise local law issues for us (e.g., serial numbers)?
* Key findings:
** Transparency language needs to be specific and clear.
** We may need to: (i) make it clear that the user is consenting to ID doc photocopying by providing it; and (ii) separately collect consent to biometric processing. Both consents must be withdrawable; if the first is withdrawn then they should be kicked from the category, if the latter is withdrawn then we should use manual methods.
** For riders (unlike drivers, where purposes are broader), it seems unlikely that we would need to retain anything beyond name, photo and gender - we should probably redact the rest. In any case, we should make it clear that what we are retaining is a copy.

Hi [~accountid:610a6c97ec92ab0070d4d852] please see summary of the external legal advise below:

# *Legal requirements for job ads*

* *No clear legal obligation to publish job ads in Estonian.* The Estonian Language Act does not expressly regulate the language of online job ads. §16(1) requires Estonian for “public notices,” but it’s unclear whether job ads qualify, and there’s *no case law* confirming this.
* *Keeleamet’s earlier official view supports non-applicability.* In its *2018 and 2019 annual reports*, Keeleamet stated that job ads on internet portals are *not “public notices”* under §16 and treated them as *private communication*, meaning complaints about foreign-language job ads were not pursued. Current stricter approach appears to be a shift without an explained rationale.
* *§17 (consumer info) likely does not apply.* It is highly questionable that employees/candidates are “consumers” under §17, which is intended for sale of goods/services per wording and legal commentary.

# *Minimum Estonian content (if §16(1) applies)*

* If job ads are treated as “public notices,” Keeleamet may expect the *full content to be available in Estonian*, not just a short summary.
* Website flexibility under §16(4) (e.g., summary, translation button, machine translation) *does not automatically extend* to “public notices,” but given the legal uncertainty, counsel suggests *checking with Keeleamet* whether a translation-tool approach would be acceptable.

h4. 3. Strategy / recommended positioning towards Keeleamet

* Respond *politely but firmly* with legal counterarguments: unclear legal basis; job ads likely not “public notices”; §17 consumer rules likely irrelevant.
* Ask Keeleamet to *explain why their practice changed* vs their 2018/2019 reports.
* Present and describe the *CVKeskus translation tool* being developed (incl. timeline) and ask Keeleamet to *confirm that this tool-based Estonian version will be accepted as compliant*.
* Optionally note that job ads require *English fluency*, supporting the business rationale for English-first ads.

h4. 4. Scope: local workaround vs wider policy change

* *LinkedIn / social media:* Keeleamet’s 2018/2019 reports indicate company social media posts are *not regulated* by the Language Act; LinkedIn also has its own translation function.
* *Careers page:* treated like a company website under §16(4), so an *Estonian summary / translation solution* should be sufficient.
* Recommendation: *do not implement a broad policy change yet*; first obtain Keeleamet’s explanation/confirmation. Wider changes may be considered only depending on their response.

# *Worst-case scenario if continuing with English-only ads*

* Keeleamet could impose a *non-compliance levy up to EUR 640*, but only after issuing a *formal warning*.
* Low risk of escalation to a *misdemeanour fine (EUR 1,300–2,600)* (possibly tied to §17), but counsel views this as *legally unjustified* given the likely non-applicability of the relevant provisions.

I would recommend to prepare reply as suggested under 3. bullet-point but please let me know if you have any additional thoughts or questions.

Hi team, 

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount. 
Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Cheers,
Afiba

*What happened*
In July 2025, Bolt Food partnered with the City of Tallinn during the Estonian National Song and Dance Celebration to promote reusable packaging among ~30k participants staying in Tallinn.

*What we did*

* 1-week awareness campaign
* On-site posters at accommodation venues
* In-app Bolt Food banner (EE & EN)
* Reusable packaging via Ringo

*Results*

* 247 orders using reusable packaging
* 397 products delivered in reusable packaging
* 23 vendors participated
* Baseline (prior 3 weeks): avg. 209 orders/week
* Result: slight uplift, not statistically significant due to short duration

*Why it matters*

* Directionally positive signal for reuse adoption during high-traffic events
* Confirms awareness + availability are key drivers
* Short campaigns alone are insufficient to shift behaviour at scale

As such, just to be clear - I am not the POC who makes the decision on this issue.

All I can say from the privacy side is that it would certainly be _preferable_ for the personal data exchange to take place exclusively between Bolt Ops OU and EOS KSI GmbH, because: (a) this will mean that the data flows are considerably easier to keep track of; and (b) the core data sharing under the agreement would not require international data transfer provisions (which are needed when personal data is being transferred outside of the EU). However, if there is a business need for Bolt/EOS entities from other countries to also be involved in the data exchange, this is also certainly something we can do - this may just require a bit more thought into some of the contractual provisions - but I cannot fully advise on this until I have full visibility of all entities involved.

Advise the customer to *check with their bank* to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. Sometimes, the payment is reversed without the bank sending a reversal notification to the customer, which might lead the user to think that the reversal has not been made.

The reversal can take up to *30 days* to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

Thank you,

Agreed on two potential scenarios on the 03/12:

{{SCENARIO 1}} - Officer attends the DEC to request data

* We have printed versions of the [Data Request Form (DRF)|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O3rw5kdzSYsBWez3Y6KpEOfRylFuKxsH/edit] available
* CS asks the officer to fill in the DRF
** CS will also ensure we have officers phone number to call them and let them know when the response is ready
* CS scans the DRF and uploads to Beehive where they also gather the requested data
* CS gets approval from CS Privacy to disclose data
* CS calls the officer so they collect the printed response

Would be good to use the government police portal to verify the officer at the DEC, but I'm not sure if this portal can be made accessible to CS?

{{SCENARIO 1}} - Officer contacts external counsel with any written requests (through email)

* External counsel verifies officers and asks them to complete the [Data Request Form (DRF)|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1O3rw5kdzSYsBWez3Y6KpEOfRylFuKxsH/edit] or completes it on their behalf
* External counsel sends the DRF to CS email
* CS gathers the requested data and places it on a google drive shared with the external counsel
* CS gets approval from CS Privacy to disclose data
* CS shares link to google drive folder with external counsel
* External counsel shares the data with the officer
