Please find attached the legal opinion from external counsel. A high-level summary is set out below.

*Key conclusions:*

* Cyprus law (Regulation (EU) 2019/6 and Law 50(I)/2024) prohibits the online listing, sale, or distribution of prescription veterinary medicinal products. The authorities are actively enforcing this prohibition against platforms, not only sellers.
* Bolt may face *administrative fines of up to* *€20,000* and, in aggravated cases, criminal exposure if prohibited products remain available on the platform after notification, as enabling ordering, payment, and delivery may be viewed as facilitating unlawful circulation.
* Once put on notice, the continued availability of such listings materially increases regulatory risk. Authorities will assess whether the platform has effective preventive, takedown, and enforcement mechanisms in place.
* Clear contractual prohibitions, allocation of compliance responsibility to merchants, and strong takedown and suspension rights are not merely advisable but necessary to mitigate exposure and demonstrate compliance-by-design vis-à-vis the Veterinary Services.

*Recommended actions:*

* Immediately prevent and remove any listings of prescription veterinary medicinal products or other veterinary products whose online sale is prohibited, and ensure effective preventive and takedown mechanisms are implemented.
* Act promptly once on notice, as continued availability of prohibited listings significantly increases regulatory risk and potential liability.
* Strengthen merchant contractual terms by introducing clear prohibitions on prohibited veterinary products, expressly referencing Regulation (EU) 2019/6 and Law 50(I)/2024, and allocating full compliance responsibility to merchants, including appropriate indemnities.
* Ensure robust enforcement and cooperation rights, including the ability to immediately remove non-compliant listings, suspend or terminate merchant accounts without prior notice, and cooperate with competent authorities when lawfully requested.

Please let us know if you have any questions or would like to discuss next steps.

Many thanks!

So, taking the logic that a profitable campaign will start from around 25-30% then we’d look at cases with campaign weight more than 30% for suspensions as those partners have caused concern most. 


Rows represent current available amounts and columns represent accurate amounts. Blue cases are overtaking both thresholds meaning that these we’d count for suspension either way. 


!Screenshot 2025-12-19 at 16.33.28.png|width=935,alt="Screenshot 2025-12-19 at 16.33.28.png"!

This suggests that we’d be including at least 81 unjustified cases more in our suspensions. 

This means we blocked hypothetically *9K eur worth GMV* in the past month. On average, we can see about *2.25K€ weekly* being the GMV impact; this makes *117K € GMV stopped* annually that we can avoid by having more information. 

Additionally, this would be 80 cases of less suspensions monthly. Not bad. 

----

*Not actioned campaign sums*
Looking at the block cases then only small portion of the campaign sums have not been deducted by us. This means that the block decisions have happened on top of deductions (which is kind of like double actioning). Justifiable would this be only for cases of career frauds and repeat abusers where we’d need to show that the re-attempts to defraud Bolt have long-term consequences.


!Screenshot 2025-12-23 at 13.23.36.png|width=530,alt="Screenshot 2025-12-23 at 13.23.36.png"!

----

*Let’s also look with an alternative lens of what we could gain as extra suspensions?*
If we were to apply the same logic and check what we are not catching then we’d see another 33 cases monthly from the actual campaign sum volume filter with the campaigns worth of 2.55K eur, however non-actioned amount of it is 831 eur for 25 drivers. 

!Screenshot 2025-12-23 at 13.17.26.png|width=410,alt="Screenshot 2025-12-23 at 13.17.26.png"!

So we’d block annually 300 drivers more for 9.9K eur of not actioned campaigns abuse and 392 drivers for 30.6K eur worth of campaigns.

Hi [~accountid:5b8d306bfa38ae2c89608b95], thank you so much for your input! Please see my additional notes below:

# Clause 2.6 - your suggestion works from the legal side. Please propose this to the partner and we can amend the contract respectively. 
# Clause 3.3.1 - agree, and the rationale from the legal side is as follows - replacing the current “best efforts” obligation with a commitment to ensure uninterrupted operation of the app would expose Bolt to disproportionate legal and financial risk, as it would effectively constitute a service guarantee that Bolt cannot fully control due to dependencies on third-party infrastructure such as cloud providers, payment processors, and telecommunications services. This would significantly lower the threshold for partner claims in the event of outages beyond Bolt’s control, increase litigation exposure, and create a non-market standard obligation inconsistent with the risk profile of a platform-based technology business. If this is not accepted by the partner, we need a commercial decision to accept such risk - however the possible damages cannot be quantified at the moment due to major range of possible issues and disruptions.
# Clause 3.13 - agree, and the rationale from the legal side is as follows - agreeing to specify a particular acquiring agreement in the partner contract would materially reduce Bolt’s operational flexibility and create avoidable legal and administrative risk. Any change of payment service provider, amendment of acquiring terms, or onboarding of additional providers would require corresponding amendments to the partner agreement, leading to delays, increased legal workload, and potential disruption of payment flows. This rigidity does not provide any tangible benefit to the partner’s performance under the agreement but increases the risk of technical non-compliance in situations where Bolt needs to react quickly to changes in its payment terms.
# Clause 4.3 - while we can technically reflect any agreed payment and settlement flow in the contract, the payment flow must first be mutually agreed between the local business team and the partner, as it constitutes the underlying commercial and technical basis on which the contractual provisions are built. Contractually committing to a structure that has not been validated from an operational and technical perspective will result in misalignment between the agreement and actual payment processes, implementation delays, increased manual interventions, and heightened risk of payment errors, disputes, and internal inefficiencies. From the legal side I will support with addition of any agreed flow in the contract after we have an internal operational alignment on that.

Advise the customer to check with their bank to confirm the release of the preauthorisation. Banks handle these releases differently, and while some are immediate, others may process it as a temporary charge that is then refunded. The reversal can take up to 30 days to complete, as pending authorisations typically expire after that time on banks end.

Unfortunately, we don't have full visibility into all the parties involved in the payment processing beyond our payment partner. Therefore, we can't track the exact status of the preauthorisation release once it has been sent.

If you need a _report_, please refer to FleetX (DriverX). If your request concerns an _invoice_, follow these steps:

3. Open the driver or fleet profile.
4. Go to the *Invoice tasks* tab.
* If you see _Invoice sum too small_, no commission invoice was generated because the driver either owed no commission or had more compensation than commission.
* If you encounter any other error, please let us know.

5. Commission invoices for the entire history of the fleet/driver are available either under *Invoice tasks* or *Partner Invoices*.

Best regards,
